1. A steel ball sinks in a container of water, but floats in a container of
mercury because               :
(A) Archimedes’ principle works only with water
(B) the steel ball displaces more mercury than water
(C) the weight of the displaced mercury is greater than the weight of the
displaced water
(D) Archimedes’ principle does not apply to round objects
(E) mercury is a chemical element and water is a chemical compound

2. Two rock specimens seem to lose the same weight when a string is
attached and submerged in water. These two specimens must have the

same               ;
(A) weight in air                          (B) weight in water
(C) weight in salt water                  (D) volume

(E) chemical and physical properties

3. Objects seem to weigh less in water than in air because they
(A) displace a volume of water            (B) sink or float
(C) exert pressure against water          (D) are affected by water pressure
(E) are not affected by air pressure

4. The pull of gravity is measured in units called

(A) kilometers                           (B) miles per hour
(C) pounds                             (D) quarts
(E) liters

LECTURE 91 : 까연과학영어  [물리학 ㅇ]

While a jet engine and a rocket engine operate on the principle on Newton’s
Third Law, they differ in that a jet must take in oxygen from the air to burn its
fuel, while a rocket must carry its own oxygen. Gases escaping under great
pressure in one direction exert a push on the engine in the opposite direction.
According to Newton’s Third Law, to each action there is an equal and opposite
reaction. You can illustrate the principle by blowing up a rubber balloon, and then
allowing the air to escape. Notice that the balloon moves forward as the air
escapes in the opposite direction.

LECTURE 92 : 자연과학영어 15) [물리학 D)

The extreme cold of last winter has made us more conscious of the need for
heat’ conservation. Americans have become aware of the fact that new fuels
should be sought and, perhaps just as important, new ways of preventing heat
loss should be developed. In the operation of engines we are concerned with the
problem of getting rid of excess heat, so that the engine does not overheat. How
is heat transferred? By  conduction,  heat energy is transferred through a
substance by increased movement of its molecules. In convection, air is heated so
that it expands and rises; it is then replaced by cooler air. When heat energy is
transferred through space, the process is called radiation. The wave motion in
radiation is similar to that of light. The higher the temperature of an object, the
greater the amount of heat it radiates. Black objects radiate more heat than light
objects at the same temperature.

LECTURE 93 : 자연과학영어 6) [지구과학]

Toward the end of the year 1973, the comet Kohoutek began to make
newspaper headlines as it moved toward the sun at great speed. Predictions were
made that it would be more spectacular than Halley’s comet, which was last seen
in 1910, as well as Ikeya-Seki of 1965 and Bennett’s of 1970.

It was first discovered in March, 1973, by a Czech astronomer, Dr. Lubos
Kohoutek, when it was still more than 500 million miles from the sun.
Astronomers reasoned that if it was visible that far out, it would probably prove
to be spectacular when it streaked to within 13 million miles of the sun on
December 28. Thus, it was expected to be the third brightest object in the sky,
after the sun and the moon.

Measurements indicated that Kohoutek’s nucleus was 20 to 25 miles across, its
coma about 10,000 miles in diameter, and its tail about 20 million miles in length.
The nucleus of a comet is thought to be composed of a clump of “dirty ice”—dust
particles, stony matter and frozen gases such as water, methane, and ammonia.
The coma is a large, hazy cloud formed when the sun’s heat liberates dust and
gases from the nucleus as the comet enters the inner part of the solar system.
The tail is a long cloud of ions and molecules that may become fluorescent under
the influence of the solar wind.

Despite the predictions made for it, the comet Kohoutek turned out to be of

such minimum brightness that few people were actually able to see it. The
reason for its disappointing appearance may be traced to the fact that it was not
the typical “dirty snowball” astronomers had predicted. Where the icy head of
Halley’s comet released streams of dust particles on melting as it approached the
sun, catching the sunlight and reflecting it in orange and yellow bands, Kohoutek
turned out to be a relatively clean, blue-white comet.
- Astronomers have identified in Kohoutek the complex methyl cyanide, which
is believed essential in star formation; this substance was previously detected
only in the vast dust clouds toward the center of the galaxy. Consequently, the
conclusion is drawn by some astronomers that comet Kohoutek originated in a
dust cloud outside of the solar system.

 Progress in chemistry was slow because of the absence of any adequate
theory to explain chemical changes, and because the earliest theory (‘alchemy’)
was so blindly optimistic as to assume that anything could be changed into
anything else. In particular, the alchemists thought that they could change a
cheap metal like lead into gold and so get rich quickly. Not until less than 200
years ago were the true foundation of chemistry laid by painstaking researches
into the nature of air and water, in fact by pure disinterested curiosity, allied to
the habit of mind which takes nothing for granted. Chemists learned that before
they could make new substances they must first discover what ordinary things
are made of ; in technical language, analysis must always precede synthesis.

[16] The body of nearly all flowering plants can be divided into two systems, the
root system which grows below ground and the shoot system which grows above
it. The typical root system anchors the plant firmly in the soil, and absorbs water
and various dissolved raw materials from it. The typical shoot system consists of
a main stem upon which are borne leaves, branch shoots, and sometimes flowers.
It should be emphasized that the words stem and shoot are not synonymous, the
word “shoot” being a collective term for both stem and leaves. The leaves are
the chief food-producing organs of the plant, making complex foods in the
presence of light by a process called photosynthesis. The stem supports the
leaves, displaying them in the light needed for photosynthesis, and also acts as
the main channel of communication between the various organs of the plant.
Water and dissolved minerals absorbed by the roots are carried in the stem to the
leaves and flowers, and foods synthesized in the leaves are conducted away
through the stem to other regions of the plant, both above and below ground,
where they are either used for growth or else stored for future use. Flowers are
organs that are concerned with the reproduction of the species by seeds.

("90 연세대 대학원)

 It is an apparent fact that computers are an important part of life today.
However, many people wonder whether humans of the future will direct the
computer or whether the opposite will be true. Perhaps we can account for this
fear as follows. It is human nature to dislike anything that causes alteration in
one’s life-style.

Since there is unanimity of opinion that computers have made and will
continue to make our lives different, this is one reason for fear. A second reason
is that, since many people do not understand the limits of computers, they are
perplexed by them and afraid of them. (1) , as computers become cheaper to
buy and easier to use, more people are procuring their own personal computers
for use at home. As a result, the public is learning that, while computers may be
good‘ (2) ’, they can only do exactly what humans tell them to do. In addition,
the smallest speck of dust in the wrong place can cause the machines to break
down. These limitations, and others, are grave ones. So, although people know
that they will never be able to have an option of a life free from computers in the
future, they are becoming less afraid of them. They are learning that computers

 Contemporary astronomy is ordinarily at least as much of an observational as a
theoretical science. Sooner or later on the basis of observation and analysis, what
astronomers detect finds its way into theory, or the theory is modified: to accept
it. Neutrino astronomy doesn’t fit this pattern. Its highly developed body of
theory grew for 30 years without any possibility of verification. And despite the
construction, finally of a string of elaborate observatories, some buried in the
earth from southern India to Utah to South Africa, the last five years as well
have produced not a single, validated observation of an extraterrestrial neutrino.

It is a testament to the persistence of the neutrino astronomers and to the
strength of their theoretical base that their intensive search for these ghost
particles still goes on.

The neutrino is a particle with a vanishingly small mass and no charge. Having
no charge, it does not interact with the fields around which most particle
detection experiments are built;it can be detected only inferentially, by
identification of the debris left following its rare interaction with matter.

Even such indirect observations need elaborate and highly sensitive equipment
which didn’t begin to go into place until about five years ago. But the goal is
worth the effort: once detected, extraterrestrial neutrinos will provide solid,
firsthand information on the sources and conditions that spawned them.

Scientists are sure of this because of the sophistication of experiments on
neutrino reactions in particle accelerators and other earth-bound apparatus. These
experiments have been refined rigorously over the years, and neutrino theory
based on them is an integral part of modern physics.

The existence of neutrinos was first postulated in the early 1930s, in order to
explain a form of radioactive decay in which a beta particle—an eletron—is
emitted. Certain quantities that physicists insist should be the same after an
interaction as before— momentum, energy, and angular momentum—could only
be conserved if another particle of  zero charge and negligible mass were
emitted.(’91 럭키금성)



===== PAGE 416 =====
414 제2부 학문분야별 독해문제 종합연습

be conserved if another particle of zero charge and negligible mass were
emitted.('91 럭키금성)

[20] The profound conceptual changes in physics in the twentieth century, the
abandonment of the doctrines of absolute space and time in Einsteins’s theory
of relativity and of causality and determinism in quantum mechanics, has
customarily led to depiction of the development of science by means of a
disjunction between ‘classical’ or ‘Newtonian’ and ‘modern’ science. This
historiographic framework is unsatisfactory, for the development of science must
be seen in a broader perspective, as a social and cultural phenomenon. The
attainment by natural science of appropriate methods of enquiry, its methods
being viewed as trained and organized common sense and its aims customarily
regarded as value-free, is a feature of its recent history. Since its emergence in
the Renaissance as a seminal feature of European intellectual life, two major
periods of scientific change stand out: first, the intellectual revolution of the
seventeenth century in which the cognitive basis of modern natural science is
traditionally seen to have been established, and second, the emergence of science
as a professional activity in the early nineteenth century when the social
structures were established which provided the basis for the integration of
science into the fabric of social life.

century were transformed into ‘physics’, ‘chemistry’, ‘biology’, ‘geology’ each

오늘날 컴퓨터가 생활의 중요한 일부임은 명백하다. 그러나 많은 사람들은 미래의 인간
들이 컴퓨터에 명령을 하게 될지 아니면 그 반대가 사실일지 궁금해하고 있다. 아마도 그
러한 TASS 다음과 같이 설명할 수 있을것 같다. 인간의 생활방식에서 변화를 일으키는
것은 어떤 것이든 싫어하는 것이 인간의 본성이다.

컴퓨터가 우리의 생활을 이전과 다르게 만들었고 앞으로도 계속 그럴 것이라는 점에는
일치되고 있기 때문에 이 점이 두려움의 한가지 이유인 것이다. 두번째 이유는, 많은 사람
들이 컴퓨터의 한계를 이해하지 못하기 때문에 컴퓨터로 인해 당황해하고 또 컴퓨터를 두
려워한다. 그러나 컴퓨터를 살 수 있게 되고 사용하기가 용이해짐에 따라 더 많은 사람들
이 가정에서 사용하가 위해 자신의 개인용 컴퓨터를 구입하고 있다. 그 결과 사람들은, 컴
THE 좋은 협력자일 수 있지만, 그것은 오직 사람이 시키는 것만 할 수 있음을 알게 되었
다. 게다가 잘못된 곳에 있는 아주 작은 먼지조각도 컴퓨터를 고장나게 할 수 있다. 이러한
또 다른 한계점들은 심각한 것들이다. 따라서 사람들은 미래에 컴퓨터가 없는 생활을 택할
수는 없겠지만 컴퓨터를 덜 두려워하게 될 것이다. 사람들은 컴퓨터가 생활의 질을 향상시
키는데 해가 없고 도움이 되는 기계가 될 수 있음을 알게 될 것이다.

Here are some storage and cleanliness guides :

*STORE FOODS IN SAFE PLACES:::----Store frozen foods in the freezer,
perishable foods to be used within a few days in the refrigerator, and canned
foods in a clean, dry place.

Keep pets, household cleaners, and other chemicals away from food. Don’t
store food near leaky pipes or seeping moisture. Control household pests (rats,
mice, roaches).

*DON’T SPREAD INFECTION:-:---Always wash your hands _ before
beginning food preparation. Teach this simple, but vital, rule to your children,
too.

Use gloves to handle food if you have any kind of skin cut or infection on your
hands. Try not to sneeze or cough into food.

*KEEP WASHING AND DRYING CLOTHS CLEAN:.:::::  Bacteria can
“loiter” in towels and cloths you use over and over, so wash kitchen linen often.
Throw out dirty or mildewed dish sponges.

*WASH HANDS AND UTENSILS IN HOT, SOAPY WATER BETWEEN
EACH STEP IN FOOD PREPARATION :-:---Bacteria present on raw meat and
poultry can get into other food if you’re not careful to wash everything they’ ve
touched before exposing another food to same surfaces and utensils. Starchy
foods and those containing dairy products are particularly vulnerable.

September 18, 1993
Dear Miss Humphrey :
I wired you this afternoon as follows:

SORRY BUT CANNOT ACCEPT
CANCELLATION OF CONTRACT
LETTER FOLLOWS

I think the situation should be cleared up at once. First, I must say that if we
had received your cancellation up to last Wednesday, we would have accepted it
without question. However, last Wednesday we started actual manufacturing of
your drugs. Labels were printed, bottles ordered, cartons purchased, and the
plant went into production.

Your wire reached me when your order was almost half finished. Parts of it
were almost entirely completed, and the rest was in various stages of
manufacture.

I’m sure you didn’t realize that we must have worked so fast. As a matter of
fact, we have been rushing in response to your request for special service.

We plan to ship your order by next week. If it will help any, we might be able
to save a day or so. However, I am sure you will now realize why we cannot
consider cancellation at this late date.

Very truly yours,

10 rules for safety when you are out

You can increase your safety on the streets and on public transport by following
a few simple rules:

1:

Da 91 = WL DO

nN

Avoid walking in badly-lit areas at night but if you must do so, walk with
confidence and be firm and positive in your actions.

. Keep your purse or wallet out of view.

. If you carry a handbag always keep it with you and never leave it open.

. If you have expensive jewellery avoid wearing it in the street.

. Carry only small amounts of cash.

. Do not carry your identification, cheque book and cheque card in the same

place.

. Do not put door keys in your bag : keep them in your pocket.
. If you are attacked, scream and shout as much as possible. Try to get away,

but be prepared to give up your valuables rather than risk injury.

. Try to avoid going out alone. Walk or travel with friends if you can.
10.

On a train, avoid carriages that are empty or have only one other person in.
On a bus or train sit near to other passengers so that you can ask for their
assistance should you need it.

 Dear Editor :

Last month our nine-year-old daughter was hit by a car. The man driving the
car was drunk at the time and didn’t stop at a stop sign.

Our little girl was in the hospital for three long weeks. My husband and I
didn’t know if she would live or die. It was a terrible time for us.

Although today she is alive, we are afraid something like that might happen
again.

Recently we heard that the punishment for the driver was only a $200 fine. He
didn’t go to jail and he didn’t lose his license. Today he is free to drive and
possibly commit the crime again. Maybe next time he will kill somebody.

We feel that traffic laws are not strict enough. Drunk drivers should pay for
their crimes. We think their licenses should be taken away. We need stricter
laws!

Yours truly,
Kathleen Johns
Phliadelphia, PA

[9]                                                                      EXECUTIVE MANSION,

Washington, January 26, 1863.
Major General Hooker:

I have placed you at the head of the Army of the Potomac. Of course I have
done this upon what appear to me to be sufficient reasons, and yet I think it best
for you to know that there are somethings in regard to which, I am not quite
satisfied with you. I believe you to be a brave and a skillful soldier, in which, of



===== PAGE 449 =====
LESSON 4 실용영어 447

course, I am right. You have confidence in yourself, which is a valuable, if not an
indispensable quality. You are ambitious, which, within reasonable bounds, does
good rather than harm. But I think that during Gen. Burnside’s command of the
army, you have taken counsel of your ambition, and thwarted him as much as you
could, in which you did a great wrong to the country, and to a most meritorious
and honorable brother officer. I have heard, in such a way as to believe it, of your
recently saying that both the army and the Government needed a Dictator. Of
course it was not for this, but in spite of it, that I have given you the command.
Only those generals who gain successes, can set up dictators. What I now ask of
you is military success, and I will risk the dictatorship. The government will
support you to the utmost of its ability, which is neither more nor less than it has
done and will do for all commanders. I much fear that the spirit which you have
aided to infuse into the army, of criticizing their Commander, and withholding
confidence from him, will now turn upon you. I shall assist you as far as I can, to
put it down. Neither you, nor Napoleon, if he were alive again, could get any
good out of any army, while such a spirit prevails in it.

And now, beware of rashness. Beware of rashness, but with energy, and
sleepless vigilance, go forward, and give us victories.

Yours very truly

A. Lincoln

DIRECTIONS: You will be given a series of paragraphs to read. Each

QUESTIONS 1~4

Philosophy is a commitment to explain and understand the universe, an
organization and clarification of the totality of human experience. It aspires to
understand everything, in its full extension and to its ultimate origins, not in its
multiplicity of detail, nor encyclopedically, but in its principles and bases.
Naturally, it cannot fulfill that aspiration adequately, just as science cannot attain
a perfect knowledge of its various spheres. In philosophical knowledge, in
scientific understanding, in the domination of natural forces, in the organization
of society, humanity advances step by step; the rapid progress in some periods
shouldn’t make us forget the extreme slowness in others. If, after much effort,
man still has not overcome the scourges of war, hunger, and disease, evils that
hurt him so cruelly, it sounds a little naive when some people blame philosophy
because it has not found the solution to these enigmas. Philosophy advances
slowly in its comprehension of the universe, with that slowness that is inevitable
in man’s greatest endeavors : perhaps its course is slower than that demonstrable
in others of man’s undertakings : because its objective could not be more vast or
more ambitious—for the intellect to encompass all of reality, including that of the
subject who is struggling to achieve this objective. This is the source of the
combination of audacity and humility that ought to characterize the philosopher
—the audacity to decide to take on the task, the humility to understand its
difficulties and resign himself beforehand to obtaining only those results that his
intellectual resources allow him in each case.

It was Robert Frost’s function to mediate between New England and the mind
of the rest of the nation, so skeptical of New England, yet so solicitous also,
eager for its welfare, willing to believe in it, but not without proofs of its
probability, its sanity, its health. Robert Frost afforded these proofs. In him the
region was born again, —it seemed never to have lost its morning vigour and
freshness ; and one felt behind his local scene the wide horizons of a man whose
sympathies and experiences were continental. He had himself discovered New
England after a boyhood in California, and he had tramped through the Carolinas
and wandered over the West ; and he knew how to say that “Yankees are what
they always were” in a way that commanded affection as well as respect. A true
folkmind, Frost was a mystical democrat, compassionately filled with a deep
regard for the dignity of ordinary living ; and he was an artist as well as a poet; a
lover of goodness and wisdom, who found them, not by seeking them, but rather
along the path of gaiety.

QUESTIONS 8- 12

John Williams is not the ringingly distinctive name that Andreas Segovia is,
but the John Williams who made his debut in Town Hall recently may make it so
for the same reason —outstanding ability on the guitar. A native of Australia who
has been living and studying in London for a decade, he came to New York via
Japan and the West Coast. This may not be according either to Horace Greeley or
Edmund Hoyle, but the discerning coterie of listeners who gave him a warm
welcome could hardly have cared less.

Study with Segovia has been among Williams’s privileges, but it also entails
some obligations—such as comparisons. The only valid one is the clear conclusion
that the youthful Williams has made enormously profitable use of his opportunity
to acquire the indispensables of superior performance on any instrument : close
identification with its internal resonance as well as its external mechanics. The
distinctively stringy, warmly vibrant sound he produces is proof not only of the
skill he commands in touch and stroke, but also of his possession of a highly
critical sense of what he wants to hear. Together they characterize the intuitive
as well as the cultivated musician, for without intuition, cultivation could hardly
have carried him so far so soon.

If there was a fault to be found with William’s debut, it would be directed at a
program that lacked a major interpretive challenge, such as the Bach Chaconne.
Bach he did play —four movements of the E-major Partita for violin (described as
the “Lute Suite IV”)—as well as Galilei (four pieces), Dowland (two short
works), and Paganini (a sonata in A). He met the requirements of Bach’s prelude
as capably as he did the twenty-four etudes of Sor on a recent recording, but the
kind of program that builds to a cumulative experience was sorely missed
(Torroba, Stephen Dodgson, Ponce, and Turina came later). Certainly he should
be heard again, and soon —preferably in matter of more weight and substance.

Near the beginning of Goethe’s career when his enthusiasm for Shakespeare
was at once the excitement of new discovery and a reflection of the
championship of the human spirit in opposition to the formalities of
Neoclassicism, he happened upon the autobiography of Gotz von Berlichingen, a
sixteenth-century robber knight who represented himself as a defender of justice
and righteousness in the midst of treacherous and Machiavellian princes and
nobles. Inspired by these idealistic sentiments, by the new patriotic spirit, and by
a strong Rousseauistic conviction in regard to the goodness of the natural



===== PAGE 465 =====
‘

464 제3부 실전대비를 위한 모의테스트

instincts of man, Goethe attempted to imitate Shakespeare’s use of historical
‘characters by writing a play about a rather obscure figure in German history.
Creating an authentic sixteenth-century. background, Goethe also projects
something of the Sturm und Drang sentiments of revolt as the rebellious hero
fights against the treachery and meanness of his age.

The play is loosely organized and often uncertain in its direction. Its fifty-eight
scenes, tragic and comic, are a deliberate flouting of time-honored principles of
good dramatic structure. But it has all the feeling of restless violence associated
with the Sturm und Drang period. Gotz rebels and takes the peasants’ side
against the artificialities and venality of a clerical court. Weisslingen is perverted
and then destroyed by associates who are incapable of perceiving the fineness of
his character. Where the spirit is pitted against the corruption of society, society
wins ; but the applause goes to the victims, and their martyrdom is an inspiration
for all mankind. Goethe knew that nobility of spirit is as rare as intelligence of
force of character; hence he was no democrat. The peasants should have a
master, but good leadership should exist for the benefit, not the exploitation, of
the people.

. QUESTIONS 24~30

Recent discoveries of the profusion of different kinds of subatomic particles
have created the major theoretic problem now confronting nuclear physicists.
The microcosmic world has changed from a simple system of electrons, protons,
and neutrons to a universe in which more than 30 fundamental particles have
been found.

One way out of the “particle mess” is to demonstrate that there really are only
a few basic particles, and that all the others arise from different states of these,
or from their interactions. None of the attempts to construct such a system,
analogous to the early attempts by chemists to render the molecular world to a
system of a few atoms, has as yet met with complete success, but the theories
are coming extremely close to their goal. Should one of them prove completely
successful in predicting the activities and mechanisms of nuclear interactions, it
would be one of the major triumphs of nuclear physics since the demonstration
that atoms are divisible.

Dr. Victor F. Weisskopf (on leave from the Massachusetts Institute of
Technology and currrently Director-General of CERN, the European Center for
Nuclear Research, Geneva, Switzerland), stated in Physics Today that “the view
that there is a large number of particles is based on a misunderstanding which is
arrived at because of three practices: each antiparticle of a given particle has
been called a new particle ; each excited state of a particle has been called a new
particle ; entities such as the light quantum have been called particles, a point
which is perhaps a matter of taste.”

Dr. Weisskopf believes that there are only two elementary particles, baryons
and leptons. Leptons are the lighter of the two types, and different forms include
the electron, muon, and neutrino. Different forms of the heavier baryon would
include protons and neutrons.

The other entities would include the “strange” particles, field quanta(mesons),
and “resonance” particles. According to Dr. Weisskopf, these may be considered



===== PAGE 468 =====
MODEL TEST ONE 467

as excited states of the baryon or as the interactions of field quanta with
themselves or baryons.

The “nuclear field” is generated by the baryons, and this is the force that holds
baryons together in an-atomic nucleus. Individual packets of energy (quanta)
compose the nuclear field. Baryons not only emit quanta, but they also react with,
absorb, and collide with them.

The particles known as pi and K mesons are examples of the field quanta.
Baryons may increase or decrease their energy through reactions with the field
quanta, and in the process they change their state. Thus lambda particles, for
example, can be created when a K meson strikes a baryon.

기원까지를 이해하고자 하는 것이다. 복잡하고 다양한 세부사항들을 백과사전식으로 이해하고
자 하는 것이 아니라 기본원리와 근간을 이루는 사항들을 이해하고자 하는 것이다. 따라서, 마치
who] 과학의 여러 분야에서 완벽한 지식에 도달할 수 없는 것과 마찬가지로 철학이 그러한 a
망을 충분히 충족시킨다는 것은 어려운 일일 수밖에 없다. 철학적 인식에 있어서나 과학적 이해
에 있어서 그리고 자연력을 지배함에 있어서나 사회를 조직함에 있어서 인간은 점진적으로 발전
해간다. 급속히 진전이 이루어졌던 몇몇 시기들만을 염두에 두고서 그밖의 다른 시기들에서는
지극히 느린 속도로 진전이 이루어졌다는 사실을 잊어서는 안된다. 적지않은 노력을 기울인 뒤
에도 여전히 인간에게 전쟁, 기아, 질병의 재앙이나 인간을 잔혹하게 유린하는 재해들이 남아있
다고 할 때, 철학이 그러한 불가사의한 일들에 대한 해결책을 제시하지 못했다고 해서 철학을 비
난하는 22 어던가 종 순진한 태도인 것처럼 보인다. 철학은 세계를 이해함에 있어서 서서히 발
전해가는데 이는 인간이 최선을 다할 경우 018 수 없이 그리될 수밖에 없는 것이다. 어쩌면 a
학의 발전속도는 인간이 시도하는 다른 분야의 일들에서 이루어지는 발전의 속도보다 더 느린
것인지도 모른다. 왜냐하면, 현실의 모든 사항을 포괄할 뿐만 아니라 철학이 추구하는 바의 목표
에 도달하고자 노력하는 주체의 모든 것까지도 포괄하는 것이 철학적 지성인 만큼, 철학의 목적

While the poll takers are most widely known for their political surverys, the
greatest part of their work is on behalf of American business. There are three
kinds of commercial surveys. One is public relations research, such as that done
for banks, which finds out how the public feels about a company. Another is
employee-attitude research, which learns from rank-and-file workers how they
really feel about their jobs and their bosses, and which can avert strikes by
getting to the bottom of grievances quickly. The third, and probably most
spectacular, is marketing research, testing public receptivity to products and
designs. The investment a company must make for a new product is
enormous — $5,000,000 to $10,000,000 for instance, for just one new product.
Through the surveys a company can discover in advance what objections the
public has to competing products, and whether it really wants a new one. These
surveys are actually a new set of signals permitting better communication
between business and the general public —letting them talk, to each other. Such
communication is vital in a complex society like our own. Without it, we would
have not only tremendous waste but the industrial anarchy of countless new
unwanted products appearing and disappearing.

The Quechua world is submerged, so to speak, in a cosmic magma that weighs
heavily upon it. It possesses the rare quality of being as it were interjected into
the midst of antagonistic forces, which in turn implies a whole body of social and
aesthetic structures whose innermost meaning must be the administration of
energy. This gives rise to the social organism known as the ay//u, the agrarian
community that regulates the procurement of food. the ay//u formed the basic
structure of the whole Inca empire.

The central idea of this organization was a kind of closed economy, just the
opposite of our economic practices, which can be described as open. The closed
economy rested on the fact that the Inca controlled both the production and
consumption of food. When one adds to this fact the religious ideas noted in the
Quechua texts cited by the chronicler Santa Cruz Pachacuti, one comes to the
conclusion that in the Andean zone the margin of life was minimal and was made
possible only by the system of magic the Quechua constructed through his
religion. Adversities, moreover, were numerous, for the harvest might fail at any
time and bring starvation to millions. Hence the whole purpose of the Quechua
administrative and ideological system was to carry on the arduous task of
achieving abundance and staving off shortages. This kind of a structure
presupposes a state of unremitting anxiety, which could not be resolved by
action. The Quechua could not do so because his primordial response to problems
was the use of magic, that is, recourse to the unconscious for the solution of
external problems. Thus the struggle against the world was a struggle against
the dark depths of the Quechua’s own psyche, where the solution was found. By

mandala as revealed by Quechua art. The Quechua empire was nothing more
than a mandala, for it was divided into four zones, with Cuzco in the center.
Here the Quechua ensconced himself to contemplate the decline of the world as

Ft. Collins, Colo.—Thunderstorms carry within them “unbelievably large”
quantities of water that are sometimes sustained in “fields” extending for more
than 10 miles, according to measurements reported here before a meeting of the
American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics.

According to Paul W. J. Schumacher, of the Aeronautical Systems Division of
Wright-Patterson Air Force base at Dayton, Ohio, and Kenneth E. Wilk, of the



===== PAGE 488 =====
MODEL TEST TWO 487

Weather Radar Laboratory, Norman, Oklahoma, water concentrations of up to 43
grams per cubic meter have been encountered by jet planes flying through such
storms.

Crewmen who flew through a strom over Oklahoma at an altitude of 29,000
feet said “it was like running into a wall of water”. The water was so dense that
it initiated a series of compressor stalls in the jet engine and caused structural
damage.

The plane’s measuring devices recorded a water content that rose from about
one-half gram per cubic meter on the edge of the storm to a maximum of 43
grams near the center.

“That was the highest reading we have ever recorded,” Mr. Schumacher told
Science Fortnightly. “It indicates an amount of water so large that some people
have questioned the findings. Our instruments are very reliable, however, and
we believe the measurements are accurate.” Readings were taken by an infrared
analyzer and amplifier specially modified and built to measure  liquid-water
content of the atmosphere (after it has been converted to vapor by the jet
engines) up to a maximum of 60 grams per cubic meter.

Aircraft flying storm missions. are subject to the hazards of ice as well as
water, according to Mr. Schumacher. Returning from such flights, research
planes sometimes show erosion and structural damage inflicted by large hail
stones. On one reported occasion, a “chase” plane flying through a thunderstorm
at an altitude of 23,000 feet was coated with an inch of rime ice in less than one
minute.

Liquid water content of thunderstorms is highly variable, and readings are
affected by the research plane’s point of penetration and the degree of maturity
of the storm. Analysis of data from 15 storms showed that “some samples of
precipitation were more than four times as heavy as the steady precipitation,” it
was stated.

QUESTIONS 21-25

A Soviet seismologist reported here that studies are now under way in central
Asia to determine whether sheer waves travelling through the earth’s crust may
be used to predict the occurrence of earthquakes.

Dr. VI. Keilis-Borok, a specialist in earthquake-wave analysis at the Institute
of the Physics of the Earth, Moscow, emphasized that the ability to predict
earthquakes is at present no more than a theoretical possibility.

Sheer (S) waves appear to slow down as they course through rock that is
under great accumulated strain, Dr. Keilis-Borok said. Since earthquakes are
believed to result from the sudden release of rock under unbearable tension, the
ability to detect the build-up of such stress through sheer-wave measurements
might be a first step toward quake prediction.

Dr. Keilis-Borok explained that the process of pinpointing the regions under
strain would be similar to triangulation in celestial navigation. Instead of fixing
on stars, seismologists would fix on crisscrossing sheer waves as they pass
through the earth. By measuring the changing speeds of the waves, regions
under stress might be located before slipping occurred.

Some disagreement exists among seismologists as to whether a precise time
for expected slippage could be established, even if the specific regions were
identified in which the requisite stress build-up is taking place. The Soviet
seismologist expressed the hope that it will become possible to measure the
accumulation of strain in the earth’s crust, and thus to determine when the stress
will reach the breaking point.

C. L. Richter, of the California Institute of Technology seismology laboratory,
says, however, that the likelihood of ever pinpointing an earthquake in time is
remote. Infinitely more than is presently known of earthquake mechanisms
would first have to be learned, he believes.

Giddy people may think the life I lead here staid and humdrum, but they are
mistaken. It is true, I hear no concerts, save those in which the thrushes are
performers in the spring morning. I see no pictures, save those painted on the
wide sky-canvas with the colours of sunrise and sunset. I attend neither rout nor
ball; I have no deeper dissipation than the tea-table ; 1 hear no more exciting
scandal than quiet village gossip. Yet I enjoy my concerts more than I would the
great London ones. I like the pictures I see, and think them better painted, too,
than those which adorn the walls of the Royal Academy ; and the village gossip
is more after my turn of mind than the scandals that convulse the clubs. It is
wonderful how the whole world reflects itself in the simple village life. The
people around me are full of their own affairs and interests; were they of
imperial magnitude, they could not be excited more strongly. Farmer Worthy is
anxious about the next market ; the likelihood of a fall in the price of butter and
eggs hardly allows him to sleep o’ nights. The village doctor —happily we have
‘only one —skirrs hither and thither in his gig, as if man could neither die nor be
born without his assistance. He is continually standing on the confines of

가를 조사하는 것이다. 다른 또 하나는 고용인의 태도에 관한 조사인데 이 조사를 통해서 하층노
동자들이 실제로 자신들의 직장과 고용주를 어떻게 생각하는가가 드러나며 따라서 노동자들의
불만을 빠른 시간내에 철저히 파악함으로써 파업을 방지할 수가 있다. 그리고 세가지 조사 방법
중에서 어쩌면 가장 중요한 것일 세번째의 것은 시장조사인데 시장조사를 통해서는 상품과 상품
의 디자인에 대한 사람들의 반응이 나타난다. 한가지의 새로운 상품을 생산하기 위해서 회사가
투자하는 금액은 엄청난 것이어서 aS 들어 말하자면 한가지의 새로운 상품을 만들어내는 데만
오백만 달러에서 일천만 달러 가량이 소요된다. 이러한 조사를 함으로써 회사는 서로 경쟁하고
있는 상품들에 대해서 사람들이 지니고 있는 Sto] 무엇인지를 사전에 알 수 있고 사람들이 실
제로 새로운 상품을 원하는 지의 여부를 사전에 알 수가 있다. 이러한 조사들은 실제로 사업체와
일반대중간의 의사소통을 보다 원활하게 해주는 일단의 새로운 신호의 기능을 한다. 사업체와
일반대중이 서로에게 자신의 의자를 표명할 수 있도록 해주는-것이다. 오늘날 우리가 살고있는
사회와 같이 복잡한 사회에서는 그러한 의사소통이 결정적인 역할을 한다. 그러한 의사소통이
이루어지지 않는다면 무수히 많은 불필요한 새 상품들이 출몰하게 되어 우리는 엄청난 낭비를 |
하게 될 것이고 산업계는 무정부상태에 빠지게 될 것이다.

QUESTIONS 1—4

The ability to express gratitude rests with the few. They are born with the
gracious tongue and the right word, but the majority of us have to acquire the art
of framing our gratitude in the most effective words.

Some go through life never passing the infantile stage of a mumble and grunt
which leaves the giver standing awkward and empty-handed, questioning the
wisdom of his gift. Others may reach the plateau where their plain, unvarnished
“Thank you” is audible but scarcely adequate for the occasion.

But those who have achieved the art —and it is an art —of expressing in words
the feeling of gratitude which is in their hearts, will leave the giver expanding
in the joy he has created, convinced that the crown jewels themselves would
have been no better choice. This pleasure alone is reward enough for the thought
and time and cost that went into the gift. It then has double value —bringing joy
to both the giver and the recipient.

QUESTIONS 8~ 14

In most corners of the world malnutrition is plainly a matter of outright
insufficiency of food for the population—where the majority of people do not
obtain enough food calories to meet minimal needs for support of physical work
and for maintenance of health. Elsewhere the problem may be not one of
insufficient calories but of lack of specific nutrients essential for health.

In Latin America, as in other places, the dread protein deficiency disease
kwashiorkor is taking its heavy toll of children’s lives: Strategic vitamins and
minerals may be lacking due to traditional diets which are nutritionally
imbalanced. Here people continue their eating pattern year after year without
knowledge of what their dietary habits are doing to themselves and to future
generations.

With a basic knowledge of nutritional needs and deficiencies, efforts could be
directed to finding food substitutes which could meet these needs. Mixtures of
vegetable proteins, like soybeans and peanuts, could provide an abundance of
cheap, useful protein where meat, eggs, and milk are not within economic reach
of large groups in the population. Efforts could also be expended on increasing
the agricultural productivity in specific regions; where large areas are given
over to relatively inefficient use as grazing land, the intensive production of
vegetable protein crops could bring remedial nutrition to an undernourished
population. Elsewhere, enrichment with specific vitamins and minerals of
traditional staple foods that are deficient in essential nutritive factors could wipe
out disabling deficiency diseases, like beriberi or pellagra, almost overnight.
Similarly, addition of minute amounts of inexpensive iodine to salt could benefit
large areas where endemic goiter has been accepted as an integral part of life for
generations.

QUESTIONS 18~ 20

A little more than a century ago, Michael Faraday, the noted British physicist,
managed to gain audience with a group of high government officials, to
demonstrate an electro-chemical principle, in the hope of gaining support for his
work.

After observing the demonstration closely, one of the officials remarked
bluntly, “It’s a fascinating demonstration, young man, but just what practical
applications will come of this?”

“I don’t know”, replied Faraday, “but I do know that 100 years from now you'll
be taxing them.”

From the demonstration of a principle to the marketing of products derived
from that principle is often a long, involved series of steps. The speed and
effectiveness with which those steps are taken are closely related to the history
of management, the art of getting things done. Just as management applies to
the wonders that have evolved from Faraday and other inventors, so it applied
some 4,000 years ago to the working of the great Egyptian and Mesopotamian
import and export firms... to Hannibal’s remarkable feat of crossing the Alps in
218 B.C. with 90,000 foot soldiers, 12,000 horsemen and a “conveyor belt” of 40
elephants... or to the early Christian Church, with its world-shaking concepts of
individual freedom and equality.

These ancient innovators were deeply involved in the problems of authority,
division of labor, discipline, unit of command, clarity of direction and the other
basic factors that are so meaningful to management today. But the real impetus
to management as an emerging profession was the Industrial Revolution.
Originating in 18th-century England, it was triggered by a series of classic
inventions and new processes, among them John Kay’s Flying Shuttle in 1733,
James Hargreaves’ Spinning Jenny in 1770, Samuel Crompton’s Mule Spinner in
1779 and Edmund Cartwright’s Power Loom in 1785.

The world at present is spending on preparations for war more than $112 billion
a year, roughly $450 per head for every man, woman, and child in the world. Let

us consider for a moment what could be done with this sum of money if it were
spent on peace and not on war. Some of it, at any rate, in the more prosperous
countries, could be spent on reduction of taxation. The rest should be spent in
ways that will, at the same time, be of benefit to mankind and a solution to the
economic problem of conversion from war industry to the expansion of peace
industries. As to this expansion, let us begin with the most elementary of all
need, namely, food. At present, the majority of mankind suffers from
undernourishment, and in view of the population explosion, this situation is likely
to grow worse in coming decades. A very small part of what is now being spent
upon armaments would rectify our predicament. Not only could the American
surplus of grain, which is now uselessly destroyed, be spent in the relief of
famine ; but by irrigation, large regions now desert could be made fertile, and by
improvement in transport, distribution from regions of excess to regions of
scarcity could be facilitated.

Housing, even in the richest countries, is often disastrously inadequate. This
could be remedied by a tiny fraction of what is being spent on missiles. Education

everywhere, but especially in the newly liberated countries of Africa and Asia,

QUESTIONS 7~ 10

Lethal rays produced by a nuclear explosion, or cosmic rays from outer space,
can be detected by special plastics.

These so-called scintillation plastics absorb nuclear rays and then re-emit them
as readily measurable electric impulses,  according to Dr. Stanley Sandler,
research chemist, Bordon Chemical Company, Philadelphia.

Dr. Sandler, one of the discoverers of a new compound for incorporation into
these plastics, told the fourth Delaware Valley Regional meeting of the American
Chemical Society that the function of the plastics in detecting radioactivity is
very much like that of a Geiger counter.

Around 1950, the first scintillation plastics were developed that could be easily
machined and were free of most of the undesirable characteristics of the natural
crystals originally used for detecting nuclear rays, Dr. Sandler reported.

Scintillation plastics are made of polystyrene or polyvinyl toluene and contain a
light- emitting compound. This gives off the energy of these rays in the form of
low intensity, almost invisible fluorescent light.



===== PAGE 539 =====

The photomultiplier tubes that pick up the rays are most sensitive to light of
longer wavelengths. Thus, many scintillation plastics also contain a “converter”
compound, or wavelength shifter, which absorbs the flourescent rays and
re-emits them at a longer wavelength where they can be amplified by the
photomultiplier tube.

Cosmic ray radiation is now being detected by 42 inch, 200 pound discs of
scintillation plastics which are incorporated in the so-called “Meson Telescope” at

the Franklin institute, he said.

Puerto Rico’s first inhabitants were Arawak Indians who come from South
America, migrating across the stepping-stone archipelago of the Lesser Antilles
to occupy the fertile island they called Borinquen. In 1493, Columbus gave the
island the name San Juan Bautista. When Ponce de Leon arrived in 1509 to
explore and colonize the island for Spain, he berthed his vessel in a safe,
beautiful harbor which he dubbed Puerto Rico. Oddly enough, harbor and
settlement came to be known as San Juan, while “Puerto Rico” applied to the
entire island. Because of its location of the strategic central portal of the New
World, where it dominated westward shipping routes of conquest and trade and
eastbound paths of ships heading home with gold and other booty from the
Spanish Main, Puerto Rico was regularly attacked and plundered. Colonists led a
precarious existence, beset by plagues, pirates, privateers and adventurers.
Among them, in 1559, was Sir Francis Drake. Three years later San Juan fell to
the Earl of Cumberland. After his defeat by illness, and subsequent departure,
the Spaniards raised powerful fortresses... La Forteleza, El Morro, San
Christobal... to defend San Juan and make it a walled city, inaccessible to
enemies from the sea. By the end of the 18th century, a polyglot population
included immigrants from the Canary Islands, Frenchmen from Haiti and
Louisiana, Spanish settlers from Santo Domingo. With them came new ideas and
methods of growing and marketing crops. Coffee and sugar became important
exports.

Under Spanish rule for over 300 years, Puerto Rico was occupied by American
troops during the Spanish-American War and ceded to the US. by the Treaty of
Paris in 1898. Since 1917 Puerto Ricians have been American citizens, and in 1952
the country achieved the status of a free commonwealth in association with the
United States.

Basically, the telephone is an instrument which permits you to talk with
someone at a distance —almost instantly —through an electrical circuit (such as a
wire). Voice signals will not travel along a wire, but electricity can travel along a
wire conductor and can be “boosted”(amplified) whenever required. The
telephone must change voice sounds into a stream of electrons capable of
traveling in an electrical circuit.

To understand how the telephone changes sound waves to electrical waves, we
must understand first what sound is. The sounds we hear are really vibrations of
air. When a person speaks, his voice sets the air in motion. These air waves—or
vibrations —are what we “hear.”

Sound vibrations can be felt, too. Maybe you have wrapped tissue paper around
a comb to make a simple musical instrument. Humming against it makes your
lips tickle. This sensation results from air causing the paper to vibrate in
response to the air waves.

But what, exactly, are sound vibrations? They are “waves” of pressure in the
air. At the high point of the waves, the air is compressed, as it is when a bicycle
pump is depressed—the air becomes more dense than normal. At the low point of
the wave, the air is less dense. Talking or singing sets up a complicated pattern
of waves, in which the air changes from denser to thinner and back again
hundreds or even thousands of times a second.

The way the telephone sends a voice along a wire is to convert the sound
pattern into a matching electrical pattern. At the other end of the line, the



===== PAGE 544 =====
MODEL TEST FOUR 543

telephone reverses the process. It changes the electrical pattern back to a
matching sound pattern.

The telephone performs this “magic” by means of transducers. Transducers
are devices which convert one form of energy, such as sound waves, into another
form, such as electrical waves.

보다는 정치가였던 사람들이다. 그들은 교리적이고 형이상학적인 까다로운 문제들보다는 사회
를 정비하는 실제적인 일에 몰두했는데 실제로도 그 일의 상당부분은 그들에게 맡겨진 것이었
다. 상당수의 종교개혁가들이 신앙고백을 하지 않았던 것과는 달리 그들은 신앙고백을 했고 그
로부터 에드워즈 학장이 SAS 때까지는 신앙고백을 실질적인 행동기반으로 삼았는데 이렇게
함에 있어서 별달리 문제될 것은 없었다. 종교상의 공인된 교리에 합리주의적인 해석방법들을
적용함으로써 신앙고백이라는 행동기반을 와해시키기 시작한 최초의 인물이었던 에드워즈는 그
의 전기출판가들이 감히 세상에 알리고자 했던 것보다 실제로는 BW 더 과감하고 광범하게 종
교교리를 합리화시켰다. 그가 대형 Aol 톱질을 가함에 따라 논쟁의 거대한 물줄기가 흘러나와
뉴우잉글랜드 전역을 뒤덮었고 이러한 자유토론으로 인해서 오늘날에 이르기까지 각기 미묘한
차이를 보이는 다양한 견해들이 존재하게 되었다. 에드워즈 자신은 거의 생각하지 못한 일이었
겠지만, BE 에머슨이나 테오도르 파커도 죠나단 에드워즈가 터트린 물줄기가 도달한 최종지점
에 위치했던 사람들이다.

핵폭발로 인해 생겨난 치명적인 방사선이나 외계에서 유입되는 우주방사선은 특수 합성수지
에 의해 탐지된다.

필라델피아 보어든 화학제품회사의 연구화학자로 있는 스탠리 샌들러 박사의 말에 의하면 이
러한 이른바 신틸레이션 합성수지는 핵방사선을 Bett 뒤 측량가능한 전기충격파로 만들어 다
시 방출한다고 한다.

이러한 합성수지의 재료 가운데 하나인 새로운 합성물질을 발견한 사람 중의 하나인 샌들러
박사는 미국화학협회의 델라웨어 밸리 지역회의에서 합성수지의 방사능 탐지기능은 가이거 계
수관의 기능과 흡사하다고 말했다.                            ,

샌들러 박사의 보고에 의하면 기계로 만들기가 용이하고 주로 핵방사선 탐지용인 천연광석이
지닌 바람직하지 못한 특성들이 거의 나타나지 않는 신틸레이션 합성수지는 1950년경에 최초로
개발되었다.

폴리스틸이나 폴리비닐 톨루엔으로 만들어지는 신틸레이션 합성수지에는 B34 (Bee) 합
성물질이 들어있다. 이 BAS 광선의 에너지를 거의 눈에 띄지 않는 저강도의 형광성 광선의 형
태로 바꾸어 발산한다.

BAS Bohs 광전배증관 파장이 긴 빛에 대해서 가장 민감하게 반응한다. 따라서 상당수
의 신틸레이션 합성수지에는 “변환기”의 기능을 하는 합성물질이나 파장변화기가 들어있는데
이것은 형광성 BAS SPAS 광전배증관에 의해 증폭될 수 있을 정도로 파장을 길게 만들
어 방출한다.

샌들러 박사의 말에 의하면 현재 우주광선을 탐지하고 있는 것은 프랭클린 연구소의 이른바
“중간자 망원경”의 재료로 사용된 길이 42인치 무게 200파운드의 신틸레이션 합성수지 디스크
라고 한다.

는 섬전체를 지칭하는 말이 되었다. 이 섬은 신대륙으로 들어가는 전략적 핵심지역에 위치하고
있었고 정복 및 무역시에 필요한 서방선로와 카리브해에서 황금과 기타 전리품을 신고 귀국하는
선박들의 동방선로에 연결되어 있었기 때문에 푸에르토리코는 수시로 침략ㆍ약탈당했다. 식민
지거주민들은 질병, 해적, 민간무장선, 투기꾼들에 시달리는 등 힘겹고 불안한 삶을 살았다. 투
기꾼들 가운데에는 1595년에 프란시스 드레이크경이 있었다. 3년후 샌주앙은 컴버랜드 백작의
수중에 들어갔고 그가 병으로 않다가 죽자 스페인인들은 샌주앙을 방어하고 해상의 적이 접근할
수 없는 성곽도시로 만들기 위해 라포르텔레짜, 엘모로, 샌크리스토발 So] 강력한 요새를 구축
했다. 18세기말에 이르러서는 다국어를 사용하는 인구의 구성원으로 카나리아 군도에서 건너온
이주민, 아이티와 루이지애나에서 건너온 프랑스인, 산토도밍고에서 건너온 스페인 정착민들이
포함되었다. 이들이 들어오면서 곡물을 재배하고 판매하는 새로운 방법들도 도입되었다. 커피와
설탕은 주요 수출품목이 되었다.

300년 이상의 기간동안 스페인의 통치를 받던 푸에르토리코는 미서전쟁중에 미군에 의해 점
령되었다가 1898년의 파리조약에 의해 미국에 양도되었다. 1917년 이후로 푸에르토리코인들은

미국시민이 되었다가 1952년에 이 나라는 미국과 연합된 자유국가의 위치를 확보했다.

기는 전선 전도체를 따라 이동할 수 있고 필요한 경우에는 언제나 “승압될”(증폭될) 수도 있다.
전화는 음성을 전기 FAS 따라 이동할 수 있는 전자파로 전환시킨다.

Asp} 어떻게 음파를 전파로 전환시키는가를 이해하려면 우선 소리가 무엇인지를 이해해야
한다. 우리에게 들리는 소리들은 사실은 공기의 진동이다. 누군가가 말을 할 때 그 음성에 의해
공기가 움직이고 이 기파 -또는 진동 -를 우리가 “듣는” 것이다.

우리는 소리의 ASS 느낄 수도 있다. 여러분은 빗에 Bho 종이를 감아 단순한 형태의 악기를
만들어 본 적이 있을 것이다. 그것에 대고 홍얼거리면 입술이 간질간질해진다. 공기에 의해 종이
가 기파에 반응해서 진동함으로써 그러한 느낌을 갖게되는 것이다.

그런데 정확히 말해서 소리의 진동이란 무엇인가? 소리의 진동은 공기의 압력의 “파동”이다.
파동이 강한 순간에 공기는 자전거의 펌프를 내리눌렀을 때 그러한 것처럼 압축되어 정상상태
이상으로 밀집된다. 파동이 약한 순간에는 공기의 응축도가 정상상태 이하로 떨어진다. 말하거
나 노래를 하면 복잡한 형태의 파동이 형성되고 그 파동 속에서 공기의 응축도가 떨어졌다가 순
식간에 다시 수백 혹은 수천배로 증가하는 것이다.

전화에 의해 음성이 AAS 따라 이동하는 AS 음성형태가 그에 상응하는 전파형태로 전환되
는 것이다. 전선의 맞은 편 마지막 지점에서 전화는 그 과정을 뒤집어 전파형태를 다시 그에 상
하는 음성형태로 전환시킨다.

전화는 변환기를 이용해서 이러한 “요술"을 부린다. 변환기는 음파와 같은 한 형태의 에너지
를 전파와 같은 다른 형태의 에너지로 전환시키는 장치이다.

The futurists broke passionately with Renaissance art. Gone was its single
center of interest, its naturalistic color, and its emphasis on humanism.’Only a
year or two later, however, Modigliani was to turn back to his ancestor,
Botticelli, and in a daring union attempt to joint this artist’s sinuous elegance to
the primitive power of newly discovered Negro art. Limiting himself almost
solely to the portraits, he juxtaposed Botticelli’s fluent line and urbane
individualism with tribal memories of Africa, miraculously inventing a language
of his own as authentic as those he combined. Wistful, frontal, lost in reverie and
loneliness, his figures transcend the stylized conventions that produced them. In
other hands, these elongated necks, ovoid heads, and flattened noses might seem
contrived, even “modernistic.” With Modigliani they are not clever technical
exercises ; they are engrossing human documents touched by humor, pathos,
sensuality, and compassion. Because his methods were easily imitated but his
content deceptively evasive, he established no school. His was a brush as
personal as the Renaissance master’s he admired. A symbol of our century,
Modigliani was, like many of his contemporaries, in love with primitive art while
yet remaining faithful to his own heritage. In fusing these two philosophies he
rarely permitted the brutality of African sculpture to submerge the refinement of
his Italian background. The transformation he effected was not due to a gentle
refurbishing of the past but to a new image he forged from two alien cultures.

QUESTIONS 7~9

During the past fifteen years, the United States and the Western powers have
been confronted with problem after problem inspired by the Communist threat to
the peace of the world. A constant struggle has taken place to maintain the peace
and yet to limit the advance of communism in various part of the world. Crises
have arisen over Berlin, the Middle East, Africa, Korea, Laos, and other parts of
the world where the cold war threatened to become more serious and deadly. In
Korea, as we know, the struggle developed into a long  and costly military
campaign which we have no desire to repeat.

In all of these crises, one pattern seems to have evolved. The Communists will
attack wherever the Western powers seem weak or disunited. If they meet with
little or only token resistance, they will maintain their pressure until they are
victorious; if they realize that they are confronted by real opposition,  they
gradually drop the struggle.

At the present time, such a situation is developing in South Vietnam. For
several months, guerrilla bands, presumably from Communist-dominated North
Vietnam and Laos have penetrated into South Vietnam and attacked villages and
rice paddies. The regular South Vietnamese forces have been unable to cope
with the irregular and sporadic raids of marauders.

To prevent the loss of South Vietnam and, ultimately, Cambodia to the Red
bloc, methods of meeting the attacks of the guerrillas must be devised. To do
this, the United States has decided to assist the regular South Vietnamese army
defeat the Viet Cong Communist forces. Our country has sent war material and



===== PAGE 563 =====
562 제3부 실전대비를 위한 모의테스트

instructors to Saigon to stop the inroads into the country made by the guerrilla
forces. The South Vietnamese army is being trained in the techniques of jungle
fighting; it is being taught to move quickly by means of helicopters and
airplanes to the area where the Viet Cong is active ; it is being instructed in the
use of modern machines and weapons.

The Viet Cong forces are small in number compared to the regular South
Vietnamese army. If they can be met in the field immediately after they attack,
and if their sources of supply can be controlled, they can easily be defeated. Our
military leaders are confident that a well-trained and highly mobile resisting
force can accomplish this.

In the past, when the Communists have met with resistance, they have
dropped their military campaigns. It is the hope of the South Vietnamese and
their mentors from the United States that this pattern will continue in South
Vietnam as soon as the guerrilla forces realize the nature of the opposition facing
them. With the withdrawal of the Viet Cong army, another pressing international
problem will have been met and solved.

myself be cast down by these portents of a failing body, nor overborne by

not by ruling over his own body, is but a ridiculous usurper. I reckon it is no loss
but an amazing boon that today I have freed myself a little more from life’s
empire.

Thus is it with old age. True, all that awaits me on the downward slope is
unfamiliar. But my heart is full of my dead friend and, gazing at the village with
eyes drained dry by my loss, I wait for love to flood through me again, like a
returning tide.

The traveler used to go about the world to encounter the native. A function of
travel agencies now is to prevent his encounter. They are always devising new
ways of insulating the tourist from the travel world. In the old traveler’s
accounts, the old colorful native innkeeper, full of sage advice and political lore,
was a familiar figure. Now he is obsolete. Today on Main Street in your home
town you can arrange transportation, food, lodging and entertainment for Rome,
Sydney, Singapore, or Tokyo.

No more chaffering. A well-planned tour saves the tourist from negotiating

_ with the natives when he get there. One reason why returning tourists nowadays
talk so much about and are so irritated by tipping practices is that these are
almost their only direct contact with the people. Even this may soon be
eliminated. The Travel Plan Commission of the International Union of Office
Travel Organization in 1958 was studying ways of standardizing tipping practices
so that eventually all gratuities could be included in the tour package. Shopping,
like tipping, is one of the few activities remaining for the tourist. It is a chink in
the wall of pre-arrangements which separates him from the country he visits. No
wonder he finds it exciting. When he shops he actually encounters natives,
negotiates in their strange language, and discovers their local business etiquette.
In a word, he tastes the thrill and “travail” which the oldtime traveler once
experienced all along the way—with every purchase of transportation, with
every night’s lodging, with every meal.

QUESTIONS 25~ 27

The whole aim of good teaching is to turn the young learner, by nature a little
copycat, into an independent, self-propelled creature who can work as his own
boss to the limit of his powers. This is to turn pupils into students, and it can be
done on any rung of the ladder of learning. When I was a child, the multiplication
table was taught from a printed sheet which had to be memorized one square at a
time—the one’s and the two’s and so on up to nine. It never occurred to the
teacher to show us how the answers could be arrived at by addition which
already knew. No one said, “Look : if four times four is sixteen, you ought to be
able to figure out, without aid from memory, what five times four is, because
that amounts to four more one’s added to the sixteen.” This would at first have
been puzzling, more complicated and difficult than memory work but once
explained and grasped, it would have been an instrument for learning and
checking the whole business of multiplication. We could temporarily have
dispensed with the teacher and cut loose from the printed table.

This is another way of saying that the only thing worth teaching any body, is a
principle. Naturally, principles involve facts and some facts must be learned
“pare” because they do not rest on any principle. The capital of Alaska is Juneau
and, so far as I know, that is all there is to it : but a European child ought to learn
that Washington is the capital of the United States without fixing firmly in his
mind the relation between the city and the man who led his countrymen to
freedom. That would be missing an association, which is the germ of a principle.
And just as a complex athletic feat is made possible by rapid and accurate
coordination, so all valuable learning hangs together and works by associations
which make sense.

QUESTIONS 28~ 30

It would be difficult today to name as many as a dozen practicing essayists in
this country ; a half dozen would be nearer to the mark. We have article writers,
novelists, poets by the thousands, but only a handful of professional writers
devoted to one of the oldest of literary forms, and still, potentially at least, one of
the most delightful and rewarding to read. From the time of Montaigne, who
fathered it, the essay has had its roots in personality ; the day may not be too far
distant when articles can be produced by supermachines, and, indeed, many of
them already have that flavor, for the article need be little more than a
marshaling of facts, fortified perhaps by the forging of an argument for or
against what the facts present. But the essay is the product of a ruminative
mind, and its value depends not upon the weight of the facts assembled (it may
not assemble any), but upon the character and quality of that mind—its
perceptiveness, its attitudes, its sharpness, its imagination. It can take off from
the most trivial incident or observation and end in the empyrean.

Why has the essay fallen into disrepute? Most magazine editors think that the
essay is an outmoded form, that it has no place in our world. Of facts we have a
surfeit, and we have not yet digested those of which we are already in
possession. Our need is not so much for the acquisition of more, as for reflection
upon those we have;not so much for arguments based upon them as for
meditations on what they suggest and what they mean. For modern man, the
acquisition of facts is like a habit —forming drug ; the more he takes, the more he
craves. Like the drug, eventually they bog him down. There are few periodicals
left in which an essay can find publication, though there is an abundant market
for factual pieces and for critical analyses commanding higher prices. Yet neither
is comparable to a first-rate essay. Still writers, like butchers, must pay their
bills.

QUESTIONS 1~8

Iona sees a hall porter with some sacking, and decides to talk with him.

“Friend, what sort of time is it?” he asks.

“Past nine. What are you standing here for? Move on.”

Iona moves on a few steps, doubles up, and abandons himself to his grief. In
less than five minutes, he straightens himself, holds his head up as if he felt
some sharp pain, and gives a tug at the reins; he can bear it no longer. “The
stables,” he thinks, and the little horse, as if it understood, starts off at a trot.

About an hour and a half later Iona is seated by a large dirty stove. Around the
stove, on the floor, on the benches, people are snoring; the air is thick and
suffocatingly hot. Iona looks on the sleepers, scratches himself, and regrets
having returned so early.

One of the cabdrivers half gets up, grunts sleepily, and stretches toward a
bucket of water,

“Do you want a drink?” Iona asks him.

“Don’t I want a drink!”

“That’s so? Your good health! but listen, mate —you know, my son is dead:::.
Did you hear? This week, in the hospital--- It’s a long story.”

Iona looks to see what effect his words have, but sees none—the young man
has hidden his face and is fast asleep again. The old man sighs, and scratches his
head. Just as much as the young one wants to drink, the old man wants to talk. Is
it nothing to tell?

“T’ll go and look after my horse,” thinks Iona; “There’s always time to sleep.
No fear of that!”

He puts on his coat, and goes to the stables to his horse ; he thinks of the corn,
the hay, the weather. When he is alone, he dares not think of his son; he can
speak about him to anyone, but to think of him, and picture him to himself, is
unbearably painful.

“Are you tucking in?”

Iona asks his horse, looking at its bright eyes, “go on, tuck in, though we’ ve
not earned oyr corn, we can eat hay.”

Iona is silent for a moment, then continues :

“That’s how it is, my old horse. There’s no more Kuzma Ionitch. Now let’s say,
you had a foal, you were the foal’s mother, and suddenly, let’s say, that foal went
and left you to live after him. It would be sad, wouldn’t it?”

QUESTIONS 9~ 14

Many harsh allegations were made against Woodrow Wilson by his enemies,
and some still survive in the folklore of today. It was said, for example, that he
wanted only flattery from his associates, that he did not take kindly to frankness
or dissent. It was said that he was a cold, distant, arrogant man who reached his
decisions, not by rational processes, but by intuition, and formed his conclusions
in isolation.

To me these allegations seem completely preposterous. They do not fit in with
any experience I ever had with him, although admittedly my contacts were
limited. That he was a man of steely determination who allowed no compromise
on what he regarded as a matter of principle is transparently true. Equally true is
the fact that he had too little appreciation of “human lubricants”; the need of
explanation, conference, and team play, the ability to keep differences of opinion
on an impersonal level. He did not suffer fools gladly —neither fools nor people
with untidy minds. There was an element of intellectual impatience in his
makeup, and more than a dash of volatile temper. It was not easy for him to
forget or forgive. In other words, he was a human being, and he had his
temperamental and physical limitations.

It was the voyageur who captured my imagination—he who carried the
tremendous loads, paddled from dawn to dark fighting waves and storms,
existing on a diet of pea soup and a daily spoonful of fat. His muscle and brawn
supplied the power for all the exploration and trade, but in spite of the harshness
of his life—the privation, suffering, and constant threat of death by exposure,
drowning, and Indian attack—he developed a nonchalance and joy in the
wilderness that has never been equaled in man’s conquest and exploitation of a
new land. These exuberant French-Canadian canoe men, with red sashes and
caps and songs in the face of monotony and disaster, were the ones who stood
out.

Their barely adequate contracts with the various fur companies proved that
profit had little to do with their choice of work, that it must have been
something else —perhaps the lure of far places, the romance and adventure of a
way of life they had never known before. Whatever the reason, they practically
deserted the villages along for the St.Lawrence for the pays d’en haute--- But in
spite of long absences from family and friends, grueling work on lakes and

What I learned in the land of the voyageurs taught me what to look for
everywhere, convinced me that history means the warmth of human associations,

people themselves who really counted. No longer did a country provide only

or gold seekers—their feelings came through: and when they did, the land

Rumor is the most primitive way of spreading stories—by passing them on
from mouth to mouth. But civilized countries in normal times have better sources
of news than rumor. They have radio, television, and newspapers. In times of
stress and confusion, however, rumor emerges and becomes rife. At such times
the different kinds of news are in competition : the press, television, and radio
versus the grapevine.

Especially do rumors spread when war requires censorship on many important
matters. The customary news sources no longer give out enough information.
Since the people cannot learn through legitimate channels all that they are
anxious to learn, they pick up “news” wherever they can and when this happens,
rumor thrives.

Rumors are often repeated even by those who do not believe the tales. There



===== PAGE 592 =====
MODEL TEST SIX 591

is a fascination about them. The reason is that the cleverly designed rumor gives
expression to something deep in the hearts of the victims—the fears, suspicions,
forbidden hopes, or daydreams which they hesitate to voice directly. Pessimistic
rumors about defeat and disasters show that the people who repeat them are
worried and anxious. Optimistic rumors about record production or peace soon
coming point to complacency or confidence —and often to overconfidence.

밝아서 어떤 결정을 내리지 않고 혼자서만 독단적으로 ASS 내렸다는 비난도 있었다.

내가 보기에 이러한 비난들은 그야말로 불합리한 것이다.내가 그와 자주 접촉해본 것은 물론
아니지만 내가 그와 만났을 때마다 느 바에 의하면 그러한 말들은 맞지 않는 말들이다. 그가
강철같은 의지를 지닌 사람이었고 그러한 만큼 그 자신이 원칙상의 문제라고 생각했던 것에 대
해서는 모든 타협을 거부했다는 말은 분명히 맞는 말이다. 그가 “인간관계에 있어서 윤활유와 같
은 것들”, 즉 해명이나 회의 및 공동 협력의 필요성, 그리고 다양한 견해차이들을 개인감정이나
사심이 없이 받아들이는 능력을 418A] AAA 것도 역시 사실이다. 그는 멍청한 사람들-
멍청한 사람들이나 생각이 흐트러져 있는 사람들-과 기꺼이 어울리고자 하지 않았다. 그는 기
질상 지적으로 미숙한 사람들을 너그럽게 보아주지 못했으며 곧잘 홍분해버리곤 했다. 그로서는
잊는다저나 용서한다는 것이 쉬운 일이 아너었다. 다시 말하자면 그는 한 사람의 인간이었고 그
러한 만큼 그에게도 기절상으로 분명히 드러나는 약점들은 있었던 것이다.

It is what happens to the snow that is complex to understand. New-fallen snow
resists being torn apart. It stays     15     . As it ages, two forces work on the
snow. One force is tension, which is simply a pull. The other force is shear,
which prevents one layer from sliding over another.

An avalanche probably starts when a buried layer fails in shear. This weak
layer is usually near the top of the monutain, where the tension is greatest. Not
only is gravity pulling on the snow, but so is the snow which is downhill. The
shear failure spreads quickly, so a large amount of snow drops at once.

QUESTIONS 9~ 13

For all its lurching and shambling imbecilities, the law—and only the law—is
what keeps our society from bursting apart at the seams, from becoming a
snarling jungle. While the law is not perfect, no other system has yet been found
for governing men except violence. The law is society’s safety valve, its most
painless way to achieve social catharsis ; any other way lies anarchy.

The law is the busy fireman that puts out society’s brush fires; that gives
people a nonphysical method to discharge hostile feelings and settle violent
differences ; that substitutes orderly ritual for the rule of teeth and claw. The
very slowness of the law, its massive impersonality, its insistence upon
proceeding according to settled and ancient rules—all this tends to cool and bank
the fires of passion and violence and replace them with order and reason. That is
a tremendous accomplishment in itself, however, a particular case may turn out.
All our fine Magna Cartas and constitutions and bills of rights and all the rest
would be nothing but a lot of archaic and high-flown rhetoric if we could not and
did not at all times have the law to buttress them, to interpret them, to breathe
meaning, and force, and life into them. Lofty abstractions about individual liberty
and justice do not enforce themselves. These things must be reforged in men’s
hearts every day. And they are reforged by the law, for every jury trial in the
land is a small daily miracle of a democracy in action.

Residents of Canton, Illinois (population 14,000), regulated their lives according
to the daily seven blasts of the town’s whistle, perched on top of the local
International Harvester plant. They awakened to the first morning whistle at 6
a.m., set their watches by it, and moved in steady, sure steps throughout the day,
alert to the whistle’s sound. The Environmental Protection Agency heard in the
whistle not the sound of a community ordering its hours but a D.B.A. (decibels
adjusted) measurement of 89.28 points higher than the limit allowed by a state
noise-pollution law slated to go into effect in February 1977.

There was already on the books a state nuisance law EPA could apply to the
whistle, so the Agency wrote plant manager Robert Nelson warning him that he
could be in violation of the new law. Nelson cooperated by promptly shutting
down the whistle. The town schedule went haywire: people were late for work,
parents got their children off to school at odd hours, and lunch and dinner did not
appear at the appointed times.

Within 48 hours after the shutdown, 7,000 persons had signed petitions
protesting the silencing of the whistle. As a consequence, it was turned back on.
Said an EPA spokesman, “We were just reacting to a complaint and seeing if we
should do anything about it. There is obviously not much nuisance if the majority
of the people like the whistle.”

But Sloth’s creators have completely revamped the options that have been
traditionally available in American cars. They have jettisoned the cigarette
lighter (a safety measure realized in the longterm sense and one that protects the
driver’s lungs), the radio, the record player,the maplight, and the air-conditioner.
What they have substituted is phenomonally ingenious.

First of all is the coin-tosser. It is a spring-operated device, tensionset to lob
quarters into toll booths. For turnpike driving it can be preset to toss a coin every
ten minutes at 60 miles an hour, which is what Frantic’s engineers have found
the average interval to be on pay roads. Negotiations are being held now with
the leading highway authorities to establish high-speed, nonstop toll booths for
autos equipped with the gadget.

The Sloth also boasts a parking detector, really a modified electronic sensor,
for street parkers. When in operation, it pings upon “hearing” parked cars with
their engines running in neutral. It has been known to find spots two blocks
away before nearer rival cruisers have been alerted to the news that a vacancy is
in the offing. It can also be adjusted, directionally, to alert the parker when a
towtruck is on location.

At least one Sloth improvement has caused a basic split among Frantic’s



===== PAGE 613 =====
612 제3부 실전대비를 위한 모의테스트

engineers. This is the squelcher. The squelcher could eliminate the most
pestiferous road nuisance in American—the car that honks at you when it is
patently clear that, because of physical or other circumstances, you can’t move
for fear of hitting the car in front of you. Some Sloths have been equipped with a
feedback control that responds to a rear honk with a jet of liquid enamel that is
sprayed on the honker’s windshield.

However, some safety experts have felt that while this could stop the honker
from honking it would also stop him from going, leading to chain honking
rearward. They have, therefore, fitted other Sloths with a recording device that
directs a stereo stream of invective at the honker. Admittedly an experimental
feature, the squelcher promises to be one of the more controversial items in
automotive circles.

QUESTIONS 24~ 27

We should also know that “greed” has little to do with the environmental crisis.
The two main causes are population pressures, especially the pressures of large
metropolitan populations, and the desire—a highly commendable one —to bring a
decent living at the lowest possible cost to the largest possible number of people.

The environmental crisis is the result of success —success in cutting down the
호 mortality of infants (which has given us the population explosion), success in

raising farm output sufficiently to prevent mass famine (which has given us
contamination by pesticides and chemical fertilizers), success in getting people
“out of the noisome tenements of the 19th-century city and into the greenery and
privacy of the single-family home in the suburbs (which has given us urban
sprawl and traffic jams). The environmental crisis, in other words, is largely the
result of doing too much of the right sort of thing.

To overcome the problems that success always creates, one must build on it.
But where to start? Cleaning up the environment requires determined, sustained
effort with clear targets and deadlines. It requires, above all, concentration of
effort. Up to now we have tried to do a little bit of everything —and tried to do it
in the headlines—when what we ought to do first is draw up a list of priorities.

QUESTIONS 28~ 30

On June 17, 1744, the commissioners from Maryland and Virginia negotiated a
treaty with the Indians of the Six Nations at Lancaster, Pennsylvania. The
Indians were invited to send boys to William and Mary College. In a letter the
next day they declined the offer as follows:

We know that you highly esteem the kind of learning taught in those Colleges,
and that the Maintenance of our young Men, while with you, would be very
expensive to you. We are convinced, that you mean to do us Good by your
Proposal ;and we thank you heartily. But you, who are wise, must know that
different Nations have different Conceptions of things and you will therefore not
take it amiss, if our Ideas of this kind of Education happen not to be the same as
yours. We have had some Experience of it. Several of our young People were
formerly brought up at the College of the Northern provinces: they were
instructed in all your Sciences; but, when they came back to us, they were bad
Runners, ignorant of every means of living in the woods... neither fit for
Hunters, Warriors, nor Counselors, they were totally good for nothing.

We are, however, not the less oblig’d by your kind Offer, tho’ we decline
accepting it; and, to show our grateful Sense of it, if the Gentlemen of Virginia
will send us a Dozen of their Sons, we will take Care of their Education, instruct
them in all we know, and make Men of them.

러자 도시의 타임 AASS 엉망이 되어버렸다. 사람들은 늦게 출근했고 부모들은 엉뚱한 시간
에 아이들을 학교로 보냈으며 점심 및 저녁식사는 예정된 시간에 이루어지지 않았다.

경적이 AAR 후 48시간도 지나지 않아서 7,000명의 사람들이 경적철거에 항의하는 탄원서에
ABS 했다. 그 결과 경적이 다시 사용되게 되었다. “우리는 단지 사람들의 불평에 대한 조치를
취한 것이고 우리가 어떤 조치를 취해야 할 것인가를 알아보았을 뿐이다. 대다수의 사람들이 경
적소리를 좋아한다면 불법적 방해에 해당될 만한 것은 별로 없음이 분명하다”고 EPAS] 대변인
은 말했다.

그런데 슬로쓰 제작자들은 전통적으로 미국의 차량에서 사용되었던 부분품들을 완전히 갈아
치워              은 담배용 라이터를 제거해버렸고(장기적인 안목에서 취해진 전조 ]이자 운
전자의 폐를 보호하기 의한 조치) 라디오, 레코드 플레이어, 7 ES (HAS), 에어콘을 없애버렸
다. 이러한 것들 대신에 그들이 사용한 것들은 그야말로 독창적인 것이다.

그러한 부속품 가운데 첫번째로 꼽을 수 있는 것은 동전투척기이다. 동전투척기는 용수철로
작동되는 장치인데, 동전이 통행료징수대 속에 던져넣어질 수 있게끔 용수철이 눌려져 있다. 유
료 고속도로에서 시속 60마일로 주행할 때 10분 간격으로 SAS 던져넣을 수 있도록 장치되어
있는 것이다. 시속 60마일에 10분의 간격이란 프랜턱 기사들에 의해 밝혀진 바 유료도로상에서
통행료를 지불하게 되는 평균시간간격이다. 동전투척장비를 갖춘 차량들을 위해서 고속의 논스
톱 통행료 징수대를 설치하기 위한, 도로공사 대표자들과의 협상이 현재 진행중에 있다.

슬로쓰의 또 다른 자랑거리로는 노상주차자들을 위한 주차탐지기가 있는데 이 탐지기는 개량
된 형태의 전자감식기이다. 이 탐지기는 작동되었을 때 기어가 중립위치에 놓인 채로 주차되어
있는 차량을 “탐지하는” 순간 핑소리를 낸다. 이 탐지기는 주차기능지점에 보다 가까이 다가가
있은      순찰차들이 가까운 곳에 빈자리가 있다는 사실을 탐지하기도 전에 두 블록이나 떨어져 있

주차지                    수 있는 것으로 알려져 있다. 이 탐지기는 견인차가 주차중일 경우 주차
자에게 방향을 ay aba) 한다.

프랜턱의 기술자들은 슬로쓰의 새로운 기능들 중의 한가지에 대해서만큼은 기본적으로 서로
엇갈리는 견해를 표명했다. 스켈쳐가 바로 그것이다. AAAS 사용하면 미국의 차량들ㅡ물리적
인 혹은 그밖의 상황하에서 앞에 있는 차량과의 충돌위험 때문에 도저히 움직일 수 없을 때 뒤에
서 경적을 울리는 차량-에 의한 매우 성가신 노상소음을 없앨 수가 있다. 슬로쓰 중에는 뒤에서
AAS 울리는 차량의 앞유리에 에나멜액을 분사해버리는 피드백식 조종장치가 부착된 차종들
이 있었다.                                                 7

그러나 안전문제 전문가들 중에는 이러한 장치가 바로 뒤에서 경적소리를 울리지 못하게 하는
반면에 뒤편의 운전자가 앞으로 나아가지 못하게 함으로써 결과적으로 후방의 차량들이 연쇄적
으로 AAS 울리게 된다고 생각한 사람들이 있었다. 그래서 그들은 슬로쓰 차량들에 녹음장치
를 부착시켜 그 장치를 통해 경적을 울리는 사람에게로 욕설이 울려퍼질 수 있게 했다. 현재로서
는 분명히 실험단계에 있는 장치인 스켈쳐는 자동차 업계에서 적지 않게 논란거리가 될 품목들
가운데 하나인 듯하다.
